This book covers AS topic 1 (information representation): number systems, binary arithmetic, character sets, images, sound and compression — examined in Paper 1. Floating-point numbers are A Level (Book 8). Cambridge uses binary prefixes (kibi = 2¹⁰, mebi = 2²⁰, gibi = 2³⁰) as well as denary prefixes (kilo = 10³, mega = 10⁶). Every calculation was checked by computer. Mark guides are our own, in the Cambridge style: B1 = one marking point, M1 = method, A1 = answer. They are not official Cambridge mark schemes.

Unit 1 of 10: Binary, Denary and Hexadecimal

Key ideas

  • Binary (base 2): place values 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1 for an 8-bit byte.
  • Denary (base 10) and hexadecimal (base 16): digits 0–9 and A–F (A = 10 … F = 15).
  • Binary → denary: add the place values where there is a 1.
  • Denary → binary: subtract the largest place values (or repeatedly divide by 2 and read remainders upwards).
  • Binary ↔ hex: split binary into groups of 4 bits (nibbles) from the right; each nibble is one hex digit.
  • Hex → denary: multiply each digit by its place value (16², 16¹, 16⁰).

Worked examples

Example 1: 1011 0110 = 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182.

Example 2: 1011 0110 → nibbles 1011 (B) and 0110 (6) → B6.

Example 3: 2AF₁₆ = 2 × 256 + 10 × 16 + 15 = 687.

10-mark exam-style question

(a) Convert 0011 1111 into denary and hexadecimal. [2]

(b) Convert the denary number 300 into binary and hexadecimal. [3]

(c) Convert the hexadecimal number 7E into binary and denary. [2]

(d) Explain why hexadecimal is often used instead of binary by programmers. [3]

Answers and mark guide:

  • (a) 63 (B1); 3F (B1).
  • (b) 1 0010 1100 (B1 + B1 for working/correct bits); 12C (B1).
  • (c) 0111 1110 (B1); 126 (B1).
  • (d) Shorter and easier to read (B1); fewer errors when writing or copying (B1); easy to convert to/from binary because each hex digit represents exactly 4 bits (B1).

Common mistakes

  1. Grouping nibbles from the left.
  2. Writing hex digit 10 as "10" instead of A.
  3. Forgetting leading zeros in a byte.
  4. Saying computers process hex (they process binary).
  5. Place value errors (16² = 256).

Quick recall

  1. Largest denary value in 8 bits (unsigned)?
  2. Hex digit for 13?
  3. Bits in a nibble?
  4. 1111 1111 in hex?
  5. Why use hex?

Answers: 1) 255. 2) D. 3) 4. 4) FF. 5) Shorter, easier to read, fewer errors.
